title: Light-Sheet Microscopy Pipelines for Mammalian Brain Connectivity Mapping Across Spatial Scales
content: Broad interest in the anatomical organization of mammalian brains has motivated recent advances in a variety of technologies for acquiring maps of their connectivity at varying spatial scales. On the microscale, dense anatomical reconstructions by serial-section electron microscopy resolve connections between neurons on the level of individual synapses. On the macroscale, imaging methods such as DTI, OCT, and x-ray tomography allow brain-wide mapping of fiber tracts and areal connectivity between brain regions. However, comprehensive maps of connectivity of individual neurons and cell types in large mammalian brains, particularly through the dense white matter of humans and non-human primates, are lacking. We have been developing approaches that bridge the micro- and macro- scales of brain connectivity by resolving and tracing individual axons in densely stained white matter, but that can be scaled to entire mammalian brains for detailed maps of projections over long distances, an approach we refer to as axonal connectomics. To this end, we have been developing histological methods based on tissue clearing and expansion microscopy techniques to fluorescently label axons throughout thick sections of mammalian brain tissue, as well as computational methods adapted from serial-section EM connectomics to align and assemble petascale 3D volumes from image data acquired from sectioned brain tissue [1]. The success of these methods for generating densely stained, thick sections of tissue which can be computationally reassembled after imaging has necessitated the development of scalable data acquisition platforms capable of high-throughput, high-resolution, volumetric imaging.
